documents.abstract: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) requires learning environments that connect conceptual instruction with authentic occupational practice. Access to workplaces, however, may be restricted by safety, cost, logistics, operational disruption and limited equipment. Immersive 360° video can represent real professional settings and support situated observation through head-mounted displays (HMDs), mobile devices or conventional screens. This paper presents a scoping review of immersive 360° video in TVET, workplace learning and related professional education. Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, the review searched Scopus, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink and ScienceDirect and identified 200 records. Following deduplication and screening, 49 publications representing 47 study clusters were included. The review mapped occupational and geographical contexts, evidence types, access devices, interaction, guidance, feedback, assessment, gamification, reported outcomes and limitations. Health and care professions accounted for 23 publications (46.9%), while industrial, engineering and production contexts accounted for eight (16.3%). HMDs were the primary or sole access mode in 33 publications (67.3%), and 30 (61.2%) incorporated at least moderate interaction. Twenty-six publications (53.1%) reported empirical interventions or comparisons, although comparator designs and outcome measures varied considerably. The literature frequently reported positive outcomes for presence, engagement, satisfaction, confidence and perceived authenticity. Findings for knowledge, professional performance and transfer were less consistent: several pedagogically structured interventions produced favourable results, whereas other comparisons found outcomes similar to conventional video or instruction. The reviewed literature does not support attributing educational value to immersion alone. Guidance, meaningful interaction, explanatory feedback, reflection and connection with practical activity emerged as recurrent features of interventions reporting favourable outcomes. The review also identified an uneven evidence base, with a strong concentration in health-professions education and short-term evaluations, with relatively limited evidence from apprenticeships, authentic workplaces and safety-critical operations. Future research should prioritise workplace and safety-critical contexts, delayed assessment, authentic performance and transfer, transparent reporting of instructional design, comparative device evaluation and pedagogically purposeful gamification.

Workforce planning in Saudi Arabia’s energy sector has traditionally focused on operations and safety, while employees’ psychological well-being and life satisfaction received far less attention. This gap is addressed in this study through the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) framework. The research examined how stress, anxiety, and depression influence life satisfaction among Saudi energy employees, and whether remote and non-remote employees differ on each of these four outcomes. The research design was cross-sectional and quantitative. Distress was captured with the DASS-21 and life satisfaction with the seven-point SWLS. The results showed that all three distress dimensions correlated negatively with life satisfaction. In the simultaneous regression, only depression remained a significant unique predictor (β = −0.456, p < .001). The results showed no significant differences between remote and non-remote employees in stress, anxiety, depression, or life satisfaction. Effect sizes were small and the directions were consistent (remote employees reported slightly less stress and slightly lower life satisfaction), suggesting the differences should not be treated as completely absent but cannot be confirmed in this sample. The findings provide sector-specific evidence for human-capital workforce planning under Saudi Vision 2030.

Background Managing mass casualty incidents (MCIs) during an active warfare environment presents unique challenges, including operating under extreme uncertainty. Traditionally, emergency communications rely on strict, hierarchical channels from prehospital services to receiving hospitals. However, informal digital communication streams, particularly instant messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram, are increasingly used within medical workflows. Despite international interest in public social media during disasters, empirical research regarding how hospital leadership echelons use informal messaging tools for real-time operational and clinical decision-making during active warfare remains sparse. Objective This study aimed to characterize the adoption of social media and instant messaging platforms as early information sources among hospital-based MCI managers during wartime and to evaluate their specific impact on real-time operational and clinical decision-making. Methods A multicenter, cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire distributed across all 24 national medical centers authorized to receive MCIs during wartime in Israel. Target respondents encompassed diverse leadership echelons, including emergency department directors, trauma service directors, trauma coordinators, charge nurses, emergency team members, and hospital executive leadership. Results Overall, 76 medical professionals representing key decision-makers across national receiving centers completed the survey. WhatsApp emerged as the most frequently used platform (median 3.0, IQR 2.00‐4.00). Although these informal channels provided rapid initial intelligence, 65.3% (49/75) of respondents encountered false information during emergency events. Consequently, 81.3% (n=61) reported routinely verifying social media data against official channels before executing major actions. Multivariate regression analysis revealed distinct pathways of influence: higher platform use intensity was strongly and independently associated with enhanced situational awareness ( P =.002) and greater operational decision-making influence ( P =.02). In addition, participants’ level of trust and reliance was associated with clinical decisions ( P =.01) and real-time team management ( P =.03). Furthermore, active platform engagement during live threat conditions was positively correlated with heightened situational awareness during missile launch alerts ( P <.001) and missile fall alerts ( P <.001). Platform use and trust behaviors remained consistent across years of professional experience, qualifications, and executive roles. Conclusions Informal digital platforms, dominated by WhatsApp, serve as vital, rapid early information channels for hospital MCI leadership during wartime emergencies. While use intensity directly enhances situational awareness and operational control during active missile threats, clinical and team management actions remain strictly contingent on trust. Given the high exposure to unverified data, formalizing structured verification protocols and incorporating informal digital communication strategies into hospital disaster preparedness frameworks are essential to optimize real-time decision-making in future large-scale health emergencies.

documents.abstract: Background: Digital exclusion is a multidimensional and relational process shaped by interactions among individuals, technologies, institutions, and wider social structures. Research on digital exclusion has expanded significantly in recent years, largely due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid digitalization of health, welfare, and public services. Yet, despite this growth, conceptualizations of digital exclusion remain fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of how digital exclusion contributes to the creation or intensification of health inequalities. Objective: This hermeneutic review aims to develop an interpretive understanding of how digital exclusion has been conceptualized across diverse bodies of literature in relation to health inequalities. Methods: We conducted a hermeneutic review using keyword searches and snowballing across PubMed, Scopus, and supplementary sources published between January 2020 and July 2025. Analysis involved repeated reading, note-taking, and comparative interpretation of each text's disciplinary field, theoretical orientation, and underlying assumptions about how digital exclusion is framed in relation to health inequalities. Knowledge users contributed throughout to ensure the developing interpretations remained relevant to policy, practice, and lived experience. Results: Thirty-one publications were included, spanning multiple disciplines and theoretical orientations. Five interpretive frames were identified: (1) inequality, which conceptualizes digital exclusion as arising from unequal social, economic, and material conditions; (2) power and social injustice, which highlights how institutional rules, governance arrangements, cultural norms, and service pathways condition who is recognized or supported, showing how digital systems can reproduce existing social hierarchies; (3) life transitions, which illustrates how exclusion shifts during periods of disruption or change, emphasizing the fluctuating conditions and vulnerabilities associated with major life changes; (4) psychobehavioral, which focuses on psychological, cognitive, and emotional responses to digital demands; and (5) sociotechnical misalignment, which frames exclusion as arising when digital systems do not align with people's routines or everyday contexts. These interpretive frames show how digital exclusion is understood through different yet overlapping explanations that emphasize structural conditions, institutional practices, life circumstances, individual experiences, and service and system design. Conclusions: This hermeneutic review identifies 5 interpretive frames that integrate diverse disciplinary perspectives on how digital exclusion contributes to health inequalities. The frames clarify the multiple, intersecting processes through which exclusion is produced and reproduced, helping to explain its persistence and uneven impacts. Our findings highlight the need for future research that examines structural and institutional mechanisms alongside lived experience and for digital health policy and practice to move beyond access- and skill-focused solutions toward approaches that address the multiple and interacting causes of digital exclusion.

Abstract Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

Background AI-driven clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly being introduced to enhance clinical decision-making, yet their adoption in health care remains limited. Research has examined technical, organizational, and contextual barriers to adoption, but less attention has been paid to how knowledge, values, and responsibility around AI-CDSS are constructed and negotiated in practice. Objective This study examines how clinicians and AI experts make sense of AI-CDSS by reanalyzing qualitative interview data through a feminist and constructivist science and technology studies (STS) perspective. Whereas the original study examined informational needs, this reanalysis asks how participants construct relevant knowledge, evaluate the value of AI-CDSS, and negotiate appropriate use and responsibility in clinical practice. Methods The authors conducted a reanalysis of semistructured interviews held in 2024 with clinicians (n=8) and AI experts (n=8) in the Netherlands. The original study focused on informational needs for AI-CDSS. For this analysis, a deductive coding framework based on European Commission guidelines for trustworthy AI was first applied, and the material was then inductively reorganized into 5 empirical themes. Subsequently, feminist and constructivist STS concepts were used as sensitizing concepts in an abductive analysis, and these concepts were brought into dialogue with the empirical themes to examine the sociotechnical relations underlying participants’ accounts. Results Situated knowledge shows that the informational needs of clinicians are not universal but relate to their roles and specific clinical contexts, with understanding oriented less toward technical transparency than toward actionable guidance, relevance, and integration into decision-making. Standpoint theory illuminates differences between stakeholder priorities: clinicians emphasize information on how to use and act on AI outputs within existing workflows, whereas AI experts focus more on providing technical characteristics and performance metrics. Tinkering captures how clinicians experiment with AI systems in practice to develop situated, lay forms of expertise. Situated value highlights that perceptions of an AI-CDSS’s worth are relational, with clinicians valuing novel, context-sensitive insights and developers prioritizing performance metrics. Finally, response-ability reveals how trust and accountability are largely delegated to institutional structures, while clinicians report limited legal, organizational, and structural support to respond meaningfully to uncertainty or errors when using AI-CDSS. Conclusions Reanalyzing the same interview material through an abductive STS approach makes sociotechnical dimensions visible that were not the focus of the original analysis. Rather than treating informational requirements as universal or adoption as primarily a matter of technical performance and communication, the findings show how knowledge, value, and responsibility are constituted through situated professional practices and institutional arrangements. Processes and considerations regarding how clinicians make sense of AI-CDSS are not universal but are shaped by social, cultural, and institutional contexts. This analytical perspective underscores the need for context-sensitive, multistakeholder strategies to support meaningful and responsible AI adoption in clinical practice.

Generative artificial intelligence is no longer confined to technical tasks; it is increasingly involved in high-stakes affairs such as leadership, fatwa, and adjudication. Existing studies generally conclude that artificial intelligence lacks ahliyyah and may therefore serve only as a tool, without explaining the eligibility required of the humans who rely on it or capturing its hidden shift from tool to authority. This study aims to formulate a concept of ahliyyah from the hadith Iżā wussida al-amru ilā gairi ahlihi and to contextualize it for the use of artificial intelligence in the amr of qiyādah, iftā’, and qaḍā’. This library research employs the taḥlīlī method of hadith study with a ma‘ānī al-ḥadīṡ approach, comprising criticism of the chain and text, linguistic and rhetorical (balāgah) analysis, examination of the commentaries, and contextualization of the concept of ahliyyat al-adā’. The findings show that the hadith is authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) and that the word wussida, derived from wisādah (cushion), depicts the amr as something leaned upon, so that in the context of artificial intelligence the demand for ahliyyah falls upon the human who leans on it. The study formulates the concept of ahliyyat al-isti‘ānah, the eligibility to seek the assistance of artificial intelligence, resting on competence independence, verification capacity, and ownership of ideas and responsibility. The concept distinguishes three positions of artificial intelligence, namely as wasīlah, as a formal muwassad ilaih, and as a de facto support, and shows that the last is the most subtle form of the death of expertise warned of in the hadith.

Generative artificial intelligence tutors produce detailed records of how learners question, reason, and revise, and these interaction traces are increasingly available to teachers and institutions. This commentary examines what happens to the evidential value of interaction traces when they are used to assess learning in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. I describe an Observability–Authenticity Paradox: the features that make interaction traces informative, such as exploration, expressed uncertainty, and error, are the features that learners have most reason to suppress or manage once they expect the traces to be evaluated. In terms of argument-based validity, such reactivity to evaluation weakens the extrapolation from interaction observed under evaluative conditions to learning activity that takes place without evaluation; it can also reduce the exploration on which learning depends. The threat is greatest when traces generated during learning are used for grading or credentialing without learners knowing when and how, and when inferences rest on behaviors that learners can choose to display or withhold. I distinguish this situation from teachers’ ongoing formative monitoring, consider whether assessment could instead reward productive failure, and explain why differential reactivity is a fairness issue in the measurement sense. I conclude by proposing three design principles (declared, episodic, and learner-owned assessment) and illustrating them with STEM tasks, drawing examples mainly from science education.

Concern has grown that students’ reliance on generative artificial intelligence (AI), and its use for academic dishonesty, may weaken self-efficacy, motivation, and academic achievement, yet evidence on these relationships is scattered across inconsistent labels. Following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR), this review mapped studies published between 2015 and 2025 that examined AI dependence or AI-related academic integrity alongside motivational constructs or academic achievement among higher education students. A Scopus search returned 172 records, of which 21 met the eligibility criteria and were charted. No eligible study predated 2024, eight were set in East Asia and none in Africa, and sixteen were cross-sectional surveys. The apparent inconsistency in the direction of the self-efficacy effect largely disappears once academic self-efficacy, which tended to protect against dependence, is distinguished from AI-specific self-efficacy, which tended to promote it. Dependence was associated with inflated self-efficacy, procrastination, and weaker learning, while associations with achievement were mixed. Amotivation and degree apathy predicted AI-assisted misconduct more strongly than AI use itself. The evidence base remains recent, geographically narrow, reliant on self-report, and almost without longitudinal or intervention research.

Social media platforms generate large volumes of multimodal content during natural disasters that can support situational awareness and humanitarian decision-making. However, effectively analyzing both textual and visual information remains challenging due to weak cross-modal alignment, severe class imbalance, noisy user-generated data, and limited labeled samples. This paper presents a unified multimodal transfer-learning framework that combines a frozen DeBERTa-v3-base text encoder with a frozen ResNet-50 image encoder through a simple late-fusion strategy for crisis-related classification. The architecture projects the unimodal features into a common 256-dimensional space, concatenates them, and feeds the resulting representation into a lightweight multi-layer perceptron classifier. The framework is evaluated on all three official tasks of the CrisisMMD v2.0 dataset. Experimental results show an accuracy of 0.76 (macro-F1 = 0.74) on the informativeness task, 0.43 (macro-F1 = 0.39) on the humanitarian categories task, and 0.69 (macro-F1 = 0.64) on the damage severity task. The model performs relatively well on classes with distinctive multimodal signatures, while residual confusion remains on semantically overlapping or visually subtle categories. For the damage severity task, which is primarily image-based, the multimodal model achieves essentially the same performance as an image-only configuration, indicating limited contribution from text. The study also acknowledges that formal text-only and image-only ablation experiments under the same protocol were not conducted, so the precise benefit of fusion cannot be rigorously quantified. Overall, the work demonstrates that a computationally efficient frozen late-fusion architecture can serve as a practical and reproducible reference point for multimodal crisis informatics under the resource constraints typical of real-world disaster response.

When a large language model supplies research annotations, the choice of model becomes an analytic degree of freedom. We ask how much that choice matters by putting 1100 task–occupation cells to nine models from three vendors and weighting their ratings with worker-reported task importance in the British Skills and Employment Surveys. Rankings are substantially more stable than levels: pairwise rank correlations range from 0.74 to 0.92, while the share of British jobs scoring above 0.5 ranges from under 0.1% to 38%. We therefore treat the rater as one dimension of a multiverse, reporting each rater-specific estimate and its range alongside a Rubin-style summary that incorporates their observed dispersion. The consequences depend on the downstream empirical design. A post-2022 pay gradient of –0.020 log points per interquartile range is negative under all nine raters, although it continues a pre-existing trend. In online vacancies, all nine raters initially produce negative post-2022 gradients; after teleworkability is given its own period path, seven produce significant positive coefficients, two produce small negative coefficients, and the pooled estimate is indistinguishable from zero. Neither application identifies an effect of generative AI. Validation against worker-reported AI use, competing exposure measures, assistant traffic and an independent task survey supports incremental predictive content validity and portability, but any bias shared across raters remains unidentified. The paper’s contribution is a procedure for exposing and carrying observed LLM-rater disagreement into empirical estimates.

documents.abstract: Small and medium-sized businesses need timely financial guidance, yet historical accounting logs record self-selected and often co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations. We formulate this setting as observational policy ranking: from pre-decision financial information, a policy selects one of 34 ledger-derived business-change categories for a target financial KPI. Using 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 firms, we introduce Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning (CAR-PL), an action-wise R-learner that operates directly on multi-hot logs and regularizes selection by observational support. We compare CAR-PL with an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references on company-disjoint held-out firms under a shared model-assisted scoring rule. CAR-PL has the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084), the T-Learner has the highest Revenue point estimate (0.085), and the contextual value model has the highest Quick Ratio point estimate (0.062). CAR-PL and the T-Learner are not statistically separated on either growth KPI in matched company-clustered comparisons, while CAR-PL selects 33–34 categories and produces less concentrated selections across the catalog. Outcome-model-only scoring retains the same KPI-level point-estimate leader or top pair, and category rankings remain similar when the all-zero treatment reference is replaced by the most common training co-action pattern. These findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs.

The construction industry remains one of the most dangerous sectors globally, with West African workers facing particular risks due to labour-intensive methods and limited regulatory enforcement. No previous systematic review has synthesized evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) standards among construction workers in West Africa. We searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, EBSCOhost, Science Direct and Google Scholar for quantitative studies published from June 2001 to August 18, 2026. Studies required extractable data on occupational health and safety compliance outcomes. Quality assessment used the JBI critical appraisal tool for cross-sectional studies. Studies rated as high risk of bias were excluded. Twelve cross-sectional studies met inclusion criteria: seven from Ghana and five from Nigeria. No eligible low- or moderate-risk studies from the other 14 West African countries were identified through this review. PPE use, access and provision varied substantially with helmet use 16.9%, hard-hat use 34.1% and respirator use of 1.7% during relevant tasks. 54.5% respondents in a Nigerian study reported that they did not wear a mask for silica-dust exposure. Welfare facilities were severely neglected, with flushable toilets on only 14.3% of sites. Safety knowledge and training were often more favourable than behavioural measures, but these constructs were not treated as equivalent to compliance. A study found that lack of safety training and inconsistent PPE use were associated with occupational injury, but the causality was not established. Factors associated with poorer compliance included younger age, lower educational level, casual employment, physical barriers and the absence of a construction‑specific regulatory framework. Evidence from Ghana and Nigeria identifies heterogeneous gaps across OHS compliance-related domains, particularly selected PPE practices, organisational implementation and welfare-facility provision. Knowledge, training, PPE availability and PPE use should not be interpreted as interchangeable compliance measures. Standardised multicountry observational studies and evaluations of proposed interventions are needed. Trial registration This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420250649740).

documents.abstract: Construction remains one of the world's most hazardous industries, with migrants comprising a substantial part of its workforce. Little evidence exists on occupational health disparities between migrant and non-migrant construction workers. This review compares occupational health outcomes between these two groups to inform equitable worker protection strategies. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched fourteen electronic databases and gray literature for studies published from January 1990 to May 2025. Eligible studies reported quantitative occupational health outcomes for both groups. Study quality was appraised using adapted Joanna Briggs Institute criteria and results were narratively synthesized. Thirty-eight studies across fifteen high-, upper-middle, and lower-middle-income countries were included, totaling 55,615 adverse health outcomes among migrant construction workers and 566,643 among non-migrant construction workers. Most studies were of low to moderate quality and were primarily conducted in high-income settings. Migrant construction workers experienced higher rates of fatal and general occupational injury than non-migrants. While migrants had excess risk for fatal falls, traumatic brain injury, heat-related mortality, and ocular trauma, they experienced lower all-cause morbidity and mortality. Patterns of non-fatal injuries, musculoskeletal disorders, mental health problems, and cardiovascular and metabolic disease were mixed. Occupational and structural factors significantly associated with morbidity and/or mortality among migrants included fewer years of employment and work experience, type of work, limited safety training and briefing attendance, and lower educational attainment. Associated socio-demographic and cultural factors included poor language proficiency, ethnicity, gender, risk-taking attitudes, and low awareness of workplace hazards; the role of age varied across studies. Migrant status is a significant determinant of occupational health in the construction sector. Strengthening labor protections for migrant workers and providing multilingual safety training are likely to reduce harm. Disaggregating occupational safety and health surveillance data by migrant status will further strengthen the evidence needed to protect the most at-risk construction workers. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42014009154.

documents.abstract: This study examined how job demands and psychological safety relate to perceived stress among professionals working in early childhood education and care. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources model, the study investigated both the individual and combined effects of workplace demands and explored the role of psychological safety as a psychosocial resource. Specifically, we focused on noise exposure, time pressure, and physical demands, which were selected a priori to capture distinct environmental, temporal, and bodily stressors characteristic of childcare settings. Data were collected through an anonymous survey of 344 childcare professionals employed in daycare centers across Germany. Hierarchical regression analyses were conducted to assess the predictive value of noise exposure, time pressure, physical demands, interaction effects among demands, and psychological safety. The results showed that time pressure and physical demands were significant positive predictors of perceived stress. In addition, the interaction between time pressure and physical demands significantly increased stress levels, indicating a cumulative effect when both demands were high. Noise exposure was not significantly associated with stress in the multivariate model. Psychological safety emerged as a significant negative predictor of stress and explained additional variance beyond the effects of job demands and their interactions. The findings highlight the importance of considering both structural working conditions and team climate in understanding occupational stress in early childhood education and care settings. Promoting psychologically safe work environments and reducing excessive job demands may contribute to improved well-being and more sustainable working conditions for childcare professionals.

This article addresses issues related to ergonomics and human factors, outlining key areas of research within this field. It emphasizes the role of analytical and optimization methods in making the most appropriate decisions in complex situations. The study examines selected publications that incorporate operations research, where the human factor plays a decisive role. The text also provides brief descriptions of the research areas covered in these publications, illustrating their diversity. For each case, the specific subject matter is explored, along with its connection to the broader field of human factors research and the methodology based on operations research.

This study aims to analyze students’ responses, enthusiasm, engagement, and cooperation through the use of the digital educational game Educaplay Froggy Jumps to support learning motivation in social studies. This study employs a qualitative, descriptive approach, in which data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews with teachers and students, and documentation of students in class IX.5 at SMP Negeri 7 Makassar. Data analysis utilized an interactive model comprising data collection, data condensation, data presentation, and drawing conclusions. The results of the study indicate that the use of the digital educational game Educaplay Froggy Jumps successfully sparked curiosity and high enthusiasm, transformed conventional learning into an enjoyable learning experience, and fostered students’ intrinsic motivation. Furthermore, group-based game-based learning has been shown to enhance dynamic collaboration through the mechanisms of peer scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). Thus, this digital medium is an effective alternative innovative learning strategy for addressing student boredom.

documents.abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal conditions (MSCs) are an important cause of pain, disability and reduced productivity among informal-sector workers, particularly market traders exposed to prolonged standing, heavy lifting, repetitive movements, and inadequate rest breaks (da Costa & Vieira, 2010; Pega et al., 2021). This study determined the prevalence of MSCs and identified their sociodemographic and occupational determinants among traders in the Rumuokoro and Choba markets in Obio-Akpor Local Government Area, Rivers State, Nigeria. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional design was employed, and 300 traders were recruited aged 30 years and above with at least six months of trading experience through random sampling across the two markets. Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires that incorporated a modified Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire and sections on sociodemographic characteristics and occupational exposures. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS Version 25, with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression at a 5% significance level. Results: The prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions was 81.7% (n=245), with the lower back (68.6%), knees (52.2%) and shoulders (44.5%) being the most affected regions. Almost half (45.3%) experienced pain daily, and 82.0% reported that pain interfered with their work. Significant sociodemographic associations were observed for gender (females: 86.2% versus males: 73.1%, p=0.012), age (p=0.001), education (p=0.001), body mass index (p=0.002), and family size (p=0.004). Occupational factors independently associated with MSCs included standing for seven or more hours daily (AOR=3.67, p=0.001), regular lifting of loads weighing more than 20 kg (AOR=2.95, p=0.027); taking regular work breaks was associated with lower odds of MSCs (AOR=0.38, p=0.004). Conclusion: Musculoskeletal conditions represent a substantial occupational health burden among traders in Obio-Akpor LGA, affecting most of the traders surveyed. Occupational exposures, including prolonged standing, heavy lifting and the absence of work breaks, were associated with MSCs. These findings highlight the importance of preventive ergonomic improvements at market level and access to appropriate healthcare services.

documents.abstract: Background Acute pesticide poisoning (APP) remains a global public health concern. Although developing countries use only a fraction of the pesticides produced worldwide, they bear a disproportionately high burden of pesticide poisoning. Pesticide use improves agricultural productivity by reducing crop losses, but it also poses substantial risks to human health. This study determined the prevalence, symptom distribution, and exposure-related risk factors for APP among pesticide handlers at a macadamia estate in Northern Malawi. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 144 eligible participants were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using a structured, pretested questionnaire after written informed consent had been obtained. The questionnaire captured: demographic characteristics, signs and symptoms of APP, and exposure-related risk factors. APP was defined using the World Health Organization APP case definition matrix. Associations between exposure-related risk factors and occupational APP were assessed using multivariable binary logistic regression. Results APP prevalence was 63.9% (95% CI: 56.1%–71.7%), and skin irritation was the most frequently reported symptom (58.5%). Exposure-related risk factors significantly associated with APP were secondary education (AOR = 11.56, 95% CI: 3.35–39.92, p < 0.001), drinking water while handling pesticides (AOR = 39.58, 95% CI: 3.07–509.80, p = 0.005), direct contact with pesticides (AOR = 5.84, 95% CI: 1.68–20.26, p = 0.005), and entering treated fields immediately after pesticide application (AOR = 5.13, 95% CI: 1.49–17.70, p = 0.01). Conclusions Nearly two-thirds of pesticide handlers at the estate met the case definition for APP, indicating a substantial occupational health burden. APP was significantly associated with secondary education, drinking water while handling pesticides, direct contact with pesticides, and entering treated fields immediately after pesticide application. To reduce occupational pesticide exposure, targeted behavioral safety interventions should strengthen safe pesticide-handling practices.

documents.abstract: Industry 5.0 shifts the focus of manufacturing automation toward human well-being, not just efficiency or output. This means task-allocation systems now have to juggle production targets, ergonomic safety, and what the workforce can realistically handle. Here, we introduce what we call the Ergonomics-Aware Human–Robot Task Allocation (EA-HRTA) problem. Picture it as a complex assignment challenge: for every task, we have to consider execution cost, whether the person or robot has the right skills, the workload each can take on, and the total ergonomic strain humans can safely handle. We turn this challenge into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model, so it runs on both quantum-annealing machines and gate-model quantum computers. We lay out three key contributions: first, we develop a penalty-based QUBO model and show exactly how to set penalty weights so it actually works. Second, we roll out a complete system where the very same QUBO gets sent both to a D-Wave-style simulated-annealing sampler and to our own lightweight, dependency-free QAOA statevector simulator. Finally, we’ve built and open-sourced a benchmarking suite that lets you see how quantum solutions perform next to a quick, greedy heuristic and a full-scale CBC integer programming baseline.. Across 60 runs spanning problem sizes from 9 to 240 binary variables, quantum annealing maintains a 100% constraint-feasibility rate at every scale tested, matching classical baselines closely on small instances (within 2% of the exact optimum at N = 9) but exhibiting a solution-quality gap that widens to roughly 140% at N = 240 under fixed penalty weights and a fixed annealing schedule. QAOA achieves competitive cost values only at the smallest instance tested (N = 9) and loses feasibility entirely by N = 16, consistent with known near-term gate-model scalability limits. We report a warm-start ablation seeding the annealer with the greedy solution, which does not yield a consistent improvement, and use this negative result to motivate an adaptive-penalty and problem-decomposition research direction. Rather than claiming a present-day quantum advantage, this paper contributes a reusable ergonomics-aware QUBO formulation, a transparent and reproducible benchmark methodology for the human-centric manufacturing community, and an honest empirical map of where current quantum optimization methods stand relative to classical practice at realistic shop-floor problem sizes.

This conceptual paper introduces Represented Present State Distinguished From Situated State, a structural distinction between the conditions that actually hold and a viewpoint’s current representation of those conditions. Either can change while the other remains fixed. Action and projection can therefore proceed from an account that is incomplete or mistaken, while their consequences depend on the situation itself. The account assesses a representation of the present through the evidence and scope supporting its claims. It asks what each instrument, report, inference, or observation establishes, when it was obtained, and which conditions it reaches. No viewpoint requires a complete representation of the situation. The distinction matters where an omitted or mistaken element changes projection, inquiry, or action. A bad outcome alone does not establish a representational error; an accurate account can also be followed by a poor decision or faulty execution. The discussion connects the distinction to Endsley’s account of situation awareness and examines two documented cases. At Three Mile Island in 1979, operators treated a relief valve as closed while it remained open, and their interpretation of the pressurizer level led them to regard the reactor core as covered. On Lubang Island, Hiroo Onoda retained a wartime representation after the war had ended, rejecting contrary reports until his former commander relieved him of duty in 1974. The cases distinguish a mistaken account of an ongoing condition from an account that persists after conditions have changed. Part of the Possibility and Counterfactual Structure series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who constructs a representation, who can challenge it, and who bears the consequences when it diverges from the situation. Its framework can inform human–AI research on state estimation, user modeling, evidence provenance, and whether systems distinguish changes in their internal accounts from changes in the conditions those accounts describe.

Public-serving institutions (government agencies, courts, health systems, social-welfare bodies, and regulators) are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to triage caseloads, allocate resources, detect fraud, and personalize services. Because these institutions exercise coercive and distributive authority over citizens who cannot easily exit the relationship, the stakes of getting AI wrong are qualitatively different from those in commercial settings. This paper surveys the advances, challenges, and future directions of responsible AI in the public sector, synthesizing scholarship on AI in government, algorithmic fairness, transparency, and AI ethics with practitioner-facing governance instruments. We first delimit what makes public-serving institutions distinctive: statutory mandates, due-process obligations, and diffuse accountability. We then map the state of the art across four dimensions (use cases, governance and policy instruments, fairness/transparency/accountability practices, and organizational capacity and procurement) and consolidate representative advances in a described table. We argue that the field has matured from principle proliferation toward operational risk management, exemplified by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the OECD AI Principles, yet a persistent gap remains between high-level commitments and verifiable practice on the ground. Core challenges include bias and equity harms, threats to legitimacy and due process, opacity and contestability, thin institutional capacity, and fragmented accountability. We conclude with a research and practice agenda emphasizing contestable-by-design systems, sociotechnical evaluation, procurement as governance, participatory oversight, and workforce capability. Responsible AI in public service is less a technical property of models than an institutional achievement sustained over time.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Software security education is still insufficiently addressed in many undergraduate computing curricula. Programs often emphasize attack-oriented activities rather than secure design practices, leaving future developers with limited skills to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. Active learning approaches, such as serious games, offer opportunities to foster engagement and practical understanding of secure development concepts. We aim to design and evaluate RiskGuard , a card-based serious game that supports the teaching of software vulnerabilities and security patterns, investigating its impact on students’ knowledge, intrinsic motivation, and learning experience. We conducted a controlled experiment with 32 undergraduate students from Systems Analysis and Development (SAD) and Information Security (IS) programs. Participants were assigned to either a traditional lecture or a lecture followed by a RiskGuard session. Learning and motivation were assessed using a Knowledge Assessment Questionnaire and the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), complemented by qualitative feedback. Our results indicate that RiskGuard supported concept reinforcement and increased students’ engagement and intrinsic motivation, although it did not outperform lecture-only instruction in immediate knowledge-assessment scores. RiskGuard shows potential as a complementary educational tool for promoting secure software design through game-based learning. This study contributes (i) the design and open resources of RiskGuard , (ii) empirical evidence on its learning and motivational effects, and (iii) insights for integrating serious games into cybersecurity and software engineering education.

Experimental laboratory work involves repetitive, labour-intensive manual procedures and strict safety protocols, making it an attractive area for Robotics and Artificial Intelligence (RAI). With research currently focused on technical innovation, there has been little work investigating the human factors of chemist-robot collaboration, and how these technologies will change the nature of work in chemistry. Understanding chemists’ requirements and perspectives is vital to the successful deployment and acceptance of RAI in laboratories. We examined the potential for robot-assisted chemistry experimentation through the perspective of future users by conducting contextual inquiries and semi-structured interviews with nine experimental chemists at various career levels with and without laboratory automation experience. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to gain a situated understanding of how their work could benefit from automation, as well as their perspectives and opinions on working alongside robots. We found that our participants are open to robot-assisted experimentation and have clear ideas for human-robot partnerships in the lab. We identified eight themes characterising chemists’ desired applications, the implementation requirements, and the perspectives on the adoption of robot-assisted experimentation. These findings show that successful acceptance of robot-assisted experimentation depends not only on technical innovation, but also on addressing the practical barriers and concerns of the chemists who will work alongside these systems. The key concern being that RAI should not constrain, but rather complement the role of the chemist in knowledge discovery. The findings contribute to a set of initial design considerations covering hardware, software, and interaction design for successful integration of RAI in experimental laboratory work.

Abstract Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to access organisational documentation, including standard operating procedures (SOPs), HR policies and institutional guidelines. However, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches that rely on free-form rewriting can introduce hallucinations and unstable trade-offs between completeness and conciseness, particularly in safety-and compliance-critical settings. Objectives: To evaluate extraction as a hallucination-resistant alternative to rewriting-based RAG, and to compare strategies that balance precision, recall and safety across document types and model scales. Methods: We compare multiple prompting strategies, including line-number-based source selection, extraction of relevant guideline sentences with explicit annotation of safety-related content, and a multi-stage pipeline that refines draft answers using supporting evidence from the source guideline. Constrained extraction strategies enable more reliable selection of clinically relevant source content, while direct verbatim copying provides a strong precision-oriented baseline. Experiments are conducted on documents of varying length (local NHS guidelines in acute care and oncology, as well as UK-wide NICE guidelines) and structures, using both frontier-scale and smaller locally deployable models. Performance is assessed using automatic metrics and via human expert evaluation of relevance and completeness. Results: Line-number selection provides the most consistent recall improvements for shorter, protocol-like guidelines across both large and small models, achieving medical-term recall of up to 95%. For substantially longer guidelines, draft-first extraction achieves the highest recall with selected frontier models, reaching up to 97%. Safety-oriented approaches improve precision but introduce systematic omissions, and multi-stage filtering further amplifies this trade-off. Conclusions: Line-number selection provides a robust alternative to rewriting-based RAG for accessing organisational documentation. Drafting-based approaches may offer additional benefits in very long-document settings. These findings highlight the importance of adapting retrieval strategies to document structure, model scale and the risks of omission.

documents.abstract: Safety of enteral nutrition (EN) and parenteral nutrition (PN) products depends on manufacturing quality and changes during storage, preparation, and administration. This critical narrative review examines microbiological, chemical, and physicochemical hazards, distinguishing finished-product measurements, experimental models, and patient outcomes. The evidence documents secondary microbial contamination, material-derived plasticizer exposure, and oxidative changes in selected formulations, while also identifying conditions in which administration introduces no measurable additional contamination. Mechanistic susceptibility of eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid to oxidation does not establish harmful exposure from contemporary commercial products. We propose Patient-Exposure-Oriented Nutritional Product Safety (PEONPS), a framework linking release quality, post-release change, terminal-line quality, and delivered exposure. Its proposed contribution is to integrate hazard-specific measurements with time-resolved administered dose and a prespecified test of whether the additional information changes a safety decision. Existing exposure studies provide precedents; PEONPS does not claim to introduce exposure assessment itself. Validation should compare its incremental value with established manufacturing, compounding, and administration controls. The framework offers a testable research agenda for targeted safety assessment, rather than a validated clinical score or a requirement for routine bedside testing. Supplementary targeted checks of official standards and selected safety-event and workflow studies were used to contextualize mechanical integrity and human factors; these searches were not intended to constitute exhaustive systematic retrieval.

Objectives Recent outbreaks of accelerated silicosis among engineered stone workers have shown that industrial processing can generate intense exposure to crystalline silica. Diatomaceous earth is widely used in cosmetic modelling facial masks and is generally regarded as low risk; however, calcination can convert its silica structure into cristobalite, a highly toxic crystalline form. We investigated silicosis in workers manufacturing cosmetic modelling facial masks using calcined diatomaceous earth. Methods Following identification of a sentinel case through occupational disease surveillance, we investigated workers employed in cosmetic modelling facial mask manufacturing. All workers had been exposed to calcined diatomaceous earth. Clinical evaluation included pulmonary function testing, chest radiography classified using international criteria and CT. Personal air sampling and bulk material analyses were conducted to characterise crystalline silica exposure. Results Among 18 workers who underwent the temporary occupational health examination, two met International Labour Organization (ILO) chest radiograph criteria for silicosis and five additional workers had low-dose chest CT (LDCT) findings consistent with silicosis despite chest radiographs not meeting the ILO profusion threshold. With the sentinel case, eight workers were identified as silicosis cases. All three chest radiograph-confirmed cases had large opacity category A on chest radiography and LDCT findings consistent with progressive massive fibrosis. Respiratory symptoms were uncommon, and pulmonary function was largely preserved. Measured cristobalite concentrations exceeded the Korean occupational exposure limit, and bulk material analysis revealed high cristobalite content. Conclusions Silicosis can occur in cosmetic manufacturing settings traditionally considered low risk and may be under-recognised when relying on chest radiography alone. Calcination of diatomaceous earth can generate hazardous crystalline silica exposures not captured by conventional industry-based classifications, supporting the need for exposure-based hazard reassessment and enhanced surveillance.

documents.abstract: Objective Shift work is an inherent characteristic of the nursing profession. Its detrimental effects extend beyond the physiological level, yet the resulting sleep-related worry is often overlooked. This study aimed to assess the level of sleep-related worry among shift-work nurses and identify factors independently associated with it. Methods A cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling was conducted among 326 shift-work nurses from January to March 2026. Data were collected using a General Information Questionnaire, the Anxiety and Preoccupation about Sleep Questionnaire, Athens Insomnia Scale, Social Support Rating Scale, General Self-Efficacy Scale, and Copenhagen Burnout Inventory. Multiple linear regression was employed to determine factors independently associated with sleep-related worry. Results The total score for sleep-related worry was 35 (28, 41). Spearman correlation analysis indicated that sleep-related worry was positively correlated with insomnia severity ( r = 0.638, p < 0.001) and occupational burnout ( r = 0.519, p < 0.001), and negatively correlated with social support ( r = −0.254, p < 0.001) and general self-efficacy ( r = −0.309, p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that insomnia severity ( β = 0.449, p < 0.001), occupational burnout ( β = 0.154, p = 0.007), general self-efficacy ( β = −0.110, p = 0.013), and use of sleep medication in the past 6 months ( β = 0.151, p < 0.001) were independently associated with sleep-related worry. However, social support was not independently associated with sleep-related worry in the multiple linear regression model. Conclusion Sleep-related worry among shift-work nurses is at a relatively high level. Interventions addressing self-efficacy, burnout, and sleep health should be incorporated into institutional occupational health policies, alongside legislative measures to protect nurses’ psychological health and ensure adequate rest and recovery.

This article examines how ecological citizenship is differentially enacted by residents in Singapore through everyday waste practices. It argues that household waste management is a key site through which the state governs environmental conduct by framing waste routines as civic responsibility and mobilising residents to sustain a highly engineered sociotechnical regime. Drawing on a stratified household survey of 672 respondents conducted between December 2024 and January 2025, complemented by interviews with residents, the study develops an Ecological Citizenship Index (ECI) based on waste-related behaviours, perceived responsibility and environmental awareness. It shows that ecological citizenship is shaped less by ethnicity or income than by unequal capacities linked to education, gendered domestic labour, work constraints, housing conditions and neighbourhood infrastructure. The Singaporean eco-citizen thus emerges as a socially differentiated subject. More broadly, the article contributes to debates on environmental governmentality and post-political environmentalism by highlighting how responsibilisation sustains urban order.

Abstract Visual Foundation Models (VFMs), such as DINO and CLIP, excel in semantic understanding of images but exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities, which limits their applicability to embodied systems. As a result, recent work has incorporated some 3D tasks (such as depth estimation) into VFM training. However, VFM performance remains inconsistent across other spatial tasks, raising the question of whether these models truly possess spatial awareness or overfit to specific 3D objectives. To address this question, we introduce the Spatial Relation Recognition Task (SpaRRTa) benchmark, which evaluates the ability of VFMs to identify static directional relations between visible objects. Unlike traditional 3D objectives that focus on precise metric prediction (e.g., surface normal estimation), SpaRRTa probes a fundamental capability underpinning more advanced forms of human-like spatial understanding. SpaRRTa generates an arbitrary number of photorealistic images with diverse scenes and fully controllable object arrangements, along with freely accessible spatial annotations. Evaluating a range of state-of-the-art VFMs, we reveal significant disparities in their ability to encode directional spatial relations. Through our analysis, we provide insights into the mechanisms that support or hinder this form of spatial awareness in modern VFMs. We hope that SpaRRTa will serve as a useful tool for guiding the development of future spatially aware visual models. Our project page can be found at https://sparrta.gmum.net/ .

documents.abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

documents.abstract: This study explored how seventh-grade students demonstrated situational interest during English reading comprehension and described how their language backgrounds appeared in their learning experiences and responses at SMP Cinta Rakyat 3 Pematangsiantar. A descriptive qualitative design involved 30 students from Class VII-F. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected students, and open-ended questionnaires completed by 30 students. The data were analyzed through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings showed that situational interest appeared through emotional response, interest-related cognitive engagement, and perceived value. Students described enjoyment and comfort during guided or shared reading, but some also experienced nervousness, fear, and hesitation during individual reading. Cognitive engagement appeared through asking questions, seeking clarification, repeating unfamiliar words, listening to pronunciation, and recalling previously encountered vocabulary. Students perceived English as useful for communication, vocabulary development, education, future employment, and understanding digital content. Their language backgrounds included Indonesian, Simalungun, Batak, Batak Toba, Malay, and Karo. Daily language use varied according to communication contexts, while previous English exposure came from formal learning, digital media, games, songs, books, films, and social interaction. The study presents language backgrounds as contextual information and does not establish a causal relationship between language background and situational interest.

Background Community health workers (CHWs) are essential to healthcare delivery in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) yet face increasing threats from extreme heat events (EHEs) due to climate change. Occupational health policies for CHWs remain fragmented globally, with CHWs receiving less attention than workers in other industries despite their critical frontline role. This scoping review aimed to identify barriers and facilitators affecting CHWs during EHEs and determine implementation strategies to support heat safety. Methods We conducted a scoping review by performing a systematic search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and grey literature published between 2000 and 2024, yielding 1,386 records. After screening, 20 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data synthesis applied the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to categorize barriers and facilitators, while the CFIR-ERIC matching tool mapped these to implementation strategies from the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy. Results CHWs in LMICs are central to climate-health responses, and also uniquely vulnerable to heat exposure. Widespread barriers to safe and effective service delivery during EHEs include physical challenges (such as dehydration, heat stress, and exhaustion), psychological stress linked to community expectations, inadequate infrastructure (notably poor cooling and inconsistent utilities), chronic underfunding restricting salaries and supplies, insufficient climate-health training, limited policymaker awareness of heat-health issues, and poor community health-seeking behaviors. Key facilitators that support CHWs include their strong community commitment and trust, deep contextual knowledge, disaster preparedness capabilities, and growing grassroots engagement in heat resilience efforts. However, CHWs remain frequently excluded from intervention design and strategic decision-making. The review identified 43 ERIC implementation strategies tailored to address the unique challenges and opportunities for supporting CHWs during EHEs. Of these, 65% served dual functions: mitigating barriers and reinforcing facilitators. Top-priority cross-cutting strategies included resource-sharing agreements, continuous training, promoting system adaptability, offering clinical supervision, creating educational materials, and coalition-building among stakeholders. Conclusions Many implementation strategies exist to both facilitate CHWs’ responding during EHEs and to protect them during those events. However, success depends on contextual adaptation, with interventions addressing local heat-health risks and socio-political contexts. These findings underline the need to take action to support CHWs during EHEs.

The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) marks a turning point in language education, accelerating the shift from traditional methodologies toward AI-enhanced learning environments. The aim of this article is to examine the impact of GenAI on language education, understood not as a complementary tool but as a linguistic and epistemological disruption that transforms processes of language production, evaluation, and acquisition. Drawing on a documentary analysis that integrates recent theoretical, empirical, and regulatory sources, the study addresses four interrelated objectives: to reorganize instructional design toward generative tasks of greater cognitive complexity; to identify pedagogical applications of GenAI through tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva, HeyGen, and other emerging GenAI systems; to redefine the teacher’s role as a critical orchestrator and AI-literate professional; and to examine the ethical and linguistic challenges posed by GenAI, including hallucination, discourse homogenization, and risks to academic integrity. The findings indicate that GenAI enhances learning only when embedded within intentional, critically mediated, and well-supervised pedagogy that preserves cognitive engagement, linguistic diversity, and educational equity.[La rápida expansión de la inteligencia artificial generativa (IAGen) marca un punto de inflexión en la enseñanza de lenguas, impulsando la transición desde métodos tradicionales hacia entornos de aprendizaje enriquecidos por IA. El objetivo de este artículo es examinar el impacto de la IAGen en la enseñanza de lenguas, entendida no como una herramienta complementaria, sino como una disrupción lingüística y epistemológica que transforma los procesos de producción, evaluación y adquisición del lenguaje. Mediante un análisis documental que integra fuentes teóricas, empíricas y normativas recientes, el estudio persigue cuatro objetivos específicos: reorganizar el diseño didáctico hacia actividades generativas de mayor complejidad cognitiva; identificar formas de implementación de la IAGen a través de herramientas como ChatGPT, Claude, NotebookLM, ElevenLabs, Canva o HeyGen; redefinir el rol docente como orquestador crítico y profesional con alfabetización en IA; y examinar los desafíos éticos y lingüísticos derivados de la IAGen, como la alucinación, la homogeneización del discurso o los riesgos para la integridad académica. Los resultados del análisis indican que la IAGen solo mejora el aprendizaje cuando se integra en una pedagogía intencional, crítica y supervisada que preserve el compromiso cognitivo, la diversidad lingüística y la equidad educativa].

documents.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence, big data, and other engineering technologies with clinical medicine has catalyzed the emergence of the interdisciplinary discipline of Intelligent Medical Engineering, which demands the cultivation of compound professionals integrating medical literacy, engineering competencies, and innovative thinking. As the core foundational course underpinning this discipline, Introduction to Basic Medicine remains a newly established offering lacking mature pedagogical paradigms and aligned experimental teaching systems. Conventional pure medical basic instruction models are misaligned with the cognitive attributes and training objectives of students with engineering backgrounds. This study developed and operationalized a full-cycle pedagogical reform framework oriented toward medical-engineering interdisciplinary integration to systematically construct students’ medical knowledge architecture, foster interdisciplinary thinking, and enhance capacities for independent learning, practical application, and innovation. This study employed action research coupled with quasi-experimental pedagogical practice. This pedagogical reform endeavor was predicated on two core innovative dimensions: the systematic integrated restructuring of interdisciplinary curricular content, and the construction of a closed-loop instructional paradigm encompassing pre-class preparatory activities, in-class interactive instruction, and post-class tiered consolidation. A diversified assessment framework integrating formative evaluation and summative examination was developed. A comprehensive set of evaluation metrics, including student academic performance, reliability analysis of survey instruments, classroom engagement metrics, and post-course interview feedback, was employed to appraise teaching effectiveness. The cross-institutional integrated pedagogical reform was associated with favorable shifts in student learning outcomes. It correlated with augmented autonomous learning efficiency, consolidated mastery of basic medical knowledge, and improved interdisciplinary cognitive competence. The empirical investigation further delineated prevailing limitations, encompassing inadequate depth of interdisciplinary practical components, suboptimal execution of differentiated tiered instruction, and ambiguous formative assessment criteria, alongside targeted optimization strategies. The medical-engineering integrated full-cycle instructional framework presents a transferable, empirically validated paradigm for foundational medical education in interdisciplinary majors implemented via cross-institutional collaborative training, and delivers a methodological reference for curriculum development and pedagogical innovation in emerging medical-engineering disciplines.

Background Postoperative complications after adult noncardiac surgery are frequent and strongly associated with mortality, prolonged morbidity, functional decline, and organizational burden. Because not all complications are preventable, failure to rescue has emerged as a central concept reflecting the capacity of healthcare organizations to recognize and treat deterioration in time. Methods We conducted a critical narrative review using SANRA as a quality self-appraisal framework. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for publications from 2000 to 2026, complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. The review focused on adult, non-obstetric patients recovering after noncardiac surgery, primarily in general surgical wards. Results Perioperative risk models, early warning scores, electronic health record-integrated and artificial intelligence-enabled systems, and continuous monitoring devices have improved the acquisition and integration of physiological and clinical information. However, prediction and detection do not themselves establish clinical effectiveness. These technologies primarily strengthen signal acquisition, recognition, and alert generation, whereas patient benefit depends on timely reassessment, diagnostic interpretation, escalation, treatment, and available response resources. Implementation studies improve process outcomes more consistently than patient-important outcomes. Benefit is most apparent when surveillance is linked to an explicit, procedure-specific diagnostic and therapeutic pathway. Human and organizational factors influence every stage of this process. Discussion Postoperative rescue is a sociotechnical process rather than a purely technological intervention. Current evidence supports linking deterioration alerts to explicit and adequately resourced response pathways, but effects on mortality, serious complications, disability, and recovery remain uncertain. Future studies should combine component-level and integrated-system evaluation while incorporating patient-important, process, and staff outcomes.

Background: Nurses experience occupational and personal stress, which can reduce well-being and life satisfaction and contribute to burnout. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of progressive relaxation exercises (PRE) on nurses’ life satisfaction, comfort, and burnout. Methods: This randomized controlled trial included nurses from a tertiary care hospital. The intervention consisted of PRE involving the sequential contraction and relaxation of major muscle groups. The intervention group performed PRE for 5 weeks, three times a week, with each session lasting 20 minutes, outside active working hours. Outcomes were assessed using the Satisfaction with Life Scale, Nurse Comfort Questionnaire, and Maslach Burnout Inventory. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square, t-tests, and repeated-measures ANOVA in SPSS 25.0. Results: After five weeks, the intervention group showed significantly higher life satisfaction (18.06±2.97 vs. 12.50±2.52, p < 0.001), total comfort (115.63±14.64 vs. 100.73±13.49, p < 0.001), and personal accomplishment (30.26±3.35 vs. 27.30±5.01, p = 0.009) scores than the control group. In contrast, emotional exhaustion (25.76±5.59 vs. 29.63±5.82, p = 0.011) and depersonalization (11.23±3.51 vs. 15.13±3.13, p < 0.001) were significantly lower in the intervention group. Conclusions/Application to Practice: PRE reduced nurses’ burnout and enhanced their life satisfaction and comfort. It can be recommended as a simple and reliable complementary method to support nurses’ well-being. Occupational health professionals can integrate brief, structured PRE sessions into workplace wellness programs, enabling nurses to perform standardized exercises independently during breaks or outside working hours. This practical approach may support nurses’ psychological well-being without disrupting patient care or workflow.
